mappings.note: 'Not a magazine' is a compound event: the other three categories counted and combined, or 100 minus 10. LO-3's count-and-combine, not LO-1's single favourable set.
The claim under test is 'more than half', so the probability 5/8 has to be placed against the midpoint of the 0-1 scale (LO-1 of C-6.2) after the favourable count is made (C-9.1-LO-1).
Identifies {5,6} as favourable within the six-outcome sample space of a die. Pure sample-space work; no compound event and no comparison to a threshold.
'Not defective' requires the complementary count 20-4 before dividing -- LO-3. Had it asked for P(defective) it would have been LO-1.
One favourable sector out of four equally likely ones. The simplest form of listing the sample space and picking the favourable outcome.
Four kings among 52 equally likely cards; the error to catch is using 26 as the denominator. Counting the sample space correctly is the whole task, LO-1.
The work is identifying which of 1-10 are prime, i.e. selecting the favourable subset of a listed sample space. LO-1.
Counts the multiples of 4 up to 40 as the favourable outcomes. Same LO-1 favourable-subset task as the prime item, with a divisibility criterion.
A single favourable count, 4 black out of 10. LO-1; no complement or union is taken.
Both counts are handed over and only the ORDER of the two probabilities is asked for, so this is placing them against each other on the scale (C-6.2-LO-1) rather than the counting of C-9.1-LO-1.
Requires sorting the six faces into primes {2,3,5} and composites {4,6} -- the favourable-subset identification of LO-1. The comparison follows immediately once the subsets are right.
'Only Maths' must be decomposed as 18 minus the 10 who take both before dividing by 40. That subtraction of an overlap is LO-3's breaking a compound event into countable pieces.
'Not a basketball medal' aggregates three categories against a total of 100 -- a complement handled by counting and combining, LO-3.
'Novel or science' is a union of two disjoint categories, counted separately then added (100+70 over 240). LO-3 exactly.
A valid vote is everything that is not NOTA, so the count is 70+40 or equivalently 120-10 -- a combined count, LO-3.
The refutation rests on the coin's two equally likely outcomes each being favourable once. Cited to LO-1 rather than C-6.2-LO-5, because fairness is assumed here, not judged from observed results.
Needs the four-outcome sample space HH, HT, TH, TT with HT and TH counted separately. C-9.1-LO-2 is not cited because no tree diagram is asked for -- the listing alone settles it.
Identifies the seven perfect squares up to 50 as the favourable outcomes. LO-1's favourable-subset task, with the trap being whether 1 and 49 are counted.

The reason statement -- probability rises with the number of favourable outcomes -- is the LO-1 principle, and judging it is what the item can actually assess. (The assertion has lost its bag composition; see the defect list.)

The reason offered is the complement rule and the assertion is a valid-vote count of 110 out of 120 -- combining counts for a compound event, LO-3. Not C-6.2-LO-1: the 0-1 scale is not what is being examined.
Bananas or oranges is a union needing a combined count of 50 (LO-3), which is then ranked against the apple probability on the scale (C-6.2-LO-1).
One straightforward count, then the real work: deciding whether 0.4 exceeds one third. Placing a probability against a stated value on the scale is C-6.2-LO-1.
Part (i) computes and ranks four single-category probabilities (LO-1); part (ii) tests 3/8 against one third on the scale (C-6.2-LO-1). No union or complement, so not LO-3.
Splits the die's faces into primes and composites and compares. Same favourable-subset identification as the MCQ form of this item; the comparison needs no threshold from the 0-1 scale.
'Did not fail' is the complement over four categories, giving 35/40 (LO-3), and the question then asks whether 0.875 exceeds 0.85 (C-6.2-LO-1).
Single-category counts for won, lost and drawn (LO-1), then part (iii) tests 7/12 against one half on the scale (C-6.2-LO-1).
Three sub-parts, all of them favourable-subset identification on the die: primes, composites, odds and evens. No threshold comparison and no compound event, so LO-1 alone.
Counts defective and good toys (LO-1) and then asks whether 9/10 exceeds 4/5, which is a placement on the scale (C-6.2-LO-1).
'Only Mathematics' again needs the overlap of 10 removed from 18 before any probability can be formed -- the decomposition step of LO-3.
Valid votes are 90+50 combined against 150 (LO-3); part (iii) then compares P(NOTA)=1/15 with one twelfth on the scale (C-6.2-LO-1).
Three single-category counts out of 120, then a ranking of them. LO-1 for the counts and C-6.2-LO-1 for ordering the results on the scale; nothing is unioned.
Parts (i)-(iii) are single-category counts (LO-1); parts (iv) 'not a suitcase' and (v) 'handbag or backpack' require the complement and the union to be counted and combined (LO-3).
Same two-part structure: three direct counts out of 150 (LO-1), then 'not vegan' and 'vegetarian or vegan' as combined counts (LO-3).
Window, aisle and middle are direct counts (LO-1); 'not a window seat' and 'aisle or middle' are the complement and union, which here coincide and are worth noticing (LO-3).
Four categories out of 250 counted directly (LO-1), with 'not books' and 'clothes or electronics' as the combined counts (LO-3). The printed key mis-simplifies 100/250; see the defect list.
Part (iii) unions sandwiches with snacks (LO-3) and part (ii) tests P(fruits) against one third on the scale (C-6.2-LO-1). The key's answer to (ii) is wrong; see the defect list.
Part (iii) is the union bike-or-scooter (LO-3); part (ii) places 3/8 against one third (C-6.2-LO-1). Part (i) is a ranking, subsumed by the latter.

Part (ii) compares one category against the combined count of two others and part (iii) is the complement of clothes -- both are count-and-combine, LO-3. Part (i) matching a category to exactly 1/5 rides on the same counts.
The range of any probability, 0 to 1. LO-1 of C-6.2 verbatim; nothing here is counted or experimental.
Certainty as the upper endpoint of the scale -- the second clause of C-6.2-LO-1.
Both statements are about the upper bound of the scale and what a probability of 1 means, which is C-6.2-LO-1's endpoint reading.
Impossibility as the lower endpoint, 0. The other half of C-6.2-LO-1's endpoint pair.
Gap-fill for the value of a certain event. Same endpoint outcome as qid:706798, in fill-in form.
The matching spans the whole scale -- 0 for an impossible die face, 1 for a certain one (C-6.2-LO-1) -- while the half and one-sixth rows need the favourable count from the sample space (C-9.1-LO-1).
The size of a die's sample space. LO-1's listing clause, reduced to a count.
Definition of the sample space, with the coin as the example. The first half of C-9.1-LO-1.
Writes out HH, HT, TH, TT and picks the two favourable to exactly one head -- both halves of LO-1. LO-2 is not cited because the listing is done directly, not through a tree.
Names the set of all outcomes. Terminology for LO-1's sample space.
Matches four experiments to sample-space sizes 2, 4, 6 and 36, so the skill is sizing the sample space including the two-stage cases. Still LO-1; no tree is drawn and no event is evaluated.
One favourable outcome of two equally likely ones. Cited to LO-1 rather than C-6.2-LO-2, because nothing contrasts it with an experimental value.
Three favourable out of eight, with the denominator being the total that must be assembled from both colours. LO-1.
The explicit theoretical-versus-experimental contrast, with an example of each. C-6.2-LO-2 word for word; LO-3 would require the behaviour as trials grow, which this item does not ask for.
Four kings out of 52 -- a favourable count in a large sample space. LO-1.
Four white out of a total of ten that must first be assembled. Same LO-1 counting task as qid:706809.
The even faces {2,4,6} as the favourable subset of the die's sample space. LO-1.
Asks for the EVENT as a set, {5,6}, before its probability -- 'identifies the outcomes favourable to a given event' is LO-1's second clause, and this item isolates it.
No counting at all: 1 minus 0.3, which rests on certainty being 1 at the top of the scale. Cited to C-6.2-LO-1 rather than C-9.1-LO-3, which is for complements obtained by counting.
Part (a) green is a direct favourable count out of 15 (LO-1); part (b) 'not yellow' combines the other two colours or subtracts from the total (LO-3).
That all outcome probabilities sum to 1 is the normalisation behind the scale's upper endpoint -- C-6.2-LO-1. No particular experiment is counted.
1 minus 0.4 for the complement of rain, again with no counting. Same reasoning as qid:706815.
